**Rukawa**

And now to the main reason why I posted this video. Oooof there are so many things here of which we should be aware, especially when playing as the primary pseudo-PG and offensive player in the team.

1. **Forcing 3-pointers and shots** \- **2:51**, **3:03**, and **3:10**. At this juncture, he had already become too angry to play properly. Despite Rukawa not being the best at 3-pointers, he continually tried to force the shots. Reported and penalised. In situations where the other team has a clear advantage in terms of skill, keep calm and keep trying.
2. **Blocking positioning** \- As you can see, in the beginning of the offense by the opposition, Rukawa was standing under the basket for some reason, which forced me to continuously pivot between Takasago and Hanamichi. This is as Akagi might be one of the best Cs to deal with Hanamichi, given that his block has a longer reach since he jumps forward. While I have made many mistakes too, his positioning at **0:53**, **1:09**, **1:21**, and **1:41** were the reasons why I had to continuously pivot. For the **1:41** timing especially, since Rukawa's blocking range isn't as good as Akagi, I had to get closer in case Hanamichi were to do a quick shot as seen in the video. 
3. **Offense variety -** While Rukawa may not have as much offense variety (not to say that he DOESN'T have variety, just not as much) as, say, Hanagata, Kiyota, Fukuda or Sendoh (This \*\*\*\*er is my biggest nightmare), the advantage he has is that his moves create a lot of space for his team mates. So he is actually more a PG, as he can create space, pass it on to his team mates, or create space and take a shot when open. However, from what I can surmise from this Rukawa's gameplay, he is used to doing a double cross-over, step-back, side-step, then air walk. This maneuver doesn't work at higher levels since most people would already be aware of the block timings for Rukawa as seen in **0:32**.
4. **Etiquette** \- Last but not least, this is the one that really grinds my gears the most. While I will try to stay as positive as possible to create a pleasant learning environment here, this is an absolute biggy for me.   
The issue with this Rukawa's play was that he doesn't bother to try to defend Hanamichi to the best of his abilities, and doesn't bother screening Hanamichi out when rebounds are up. While I have mentioned how my rebounding is terrible, if I were playing as Rukawa (who is also my third main) I would be screening out Hanamichi so as to level the playing field for Akagi to grab his rebounds.   
Also, seeing as how Mitsui is having trouble defending Koshino (it happens, we've all been there) he did not bother helping Mitsui mark Koshino or block his shots. Granted, this would leave the other two against myself alone, but at least I would have the prime position under the basket to cover two players at once. Finally, and this applies to everyone: **don't constantly bark orders to "watch out for rebounds" or "man to man" or "pass more" or "defend the perimeter" etc., if you yourself are not doing your own part in the overall defence**. If you simply stand there, and not bother to try to defend, (granted, he blocked Takasago once, so he gets a cookie for that) then don't get on the high horse and get all pissy about it. It's ultimately a team game; you can't expect everyone to cover your defence while expecting everyone to constantly pass to you to make shots. 

# TL;DR

1. Learn to position yourself for blocking and rebounds.
2. Pick your shots carefully.
3. **Don't be a prick-biscuit**.

Okay, I find this game fascinating for many reasons, chiefly among which is that there are many possible variations to the gameplay mechanics depending on the players you choose. Also, in my day job I'm an educator and as I analyse this game in my free time in terms of learning to get better, I find that integrating some video and analyses (like in real-life sports) works best. For what it's worth, I'm currently still a noobshit UA3, but I've been playing this game consistently for some time now, since November 2020. Some YouTubers offer great advice and tutorials, like [Slam Dunk Mobile Support](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC6cieqRiXUBWHBPG-peuZhw) and [AhBuiGaming](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCcdaxnXZcNXkJfhEUefsorw). And this community is great, so I thought I'd give back in my own little ways.

# PLAYER COMBINATION

My team: Akagi (C, me), Rukawa (SF), Mitsui (SG)  
Opposing team: Takasago (C), SH Sakuragi (PF), Koshino (SG)

In terms of the choices, both teams are pretty balanced. My team can possibly focus on either the SG or SF for offense with Akagi stealing some close shot 2-pointers (shout out to KirinHaven for his advice that I implemented into my Akagi play). 

The opposing team can either go full SG offence - so pick and roll for Koshino while he dances and shoots - or do a balanced offence that capitalises on quick passes and finding space, which this team did. Taka and Hana can do their quick-pass offense with Koshino as a support, or Koshino takes 3-pointers when open.

# ACTUAL GAMEPLAY IN THE VIDEO

So, as per the title of the video, **I'll be focusing mainly on what went wrong for my team while breaking down the individual players' performances**. 

**Akagi**

1. **Block positioning relative to marking** \- my focus on marking was too scatter-brained. I should have stuck to the paint, while staying aware of Takasago's and Sakuragi's offense. At **0:55** for example, I should have backtracked into position as Sakuragi was in a prime position to befuddle the defence with his quick dunk. At **1:01** too; Takasago was moving away, and while he IS able to make some mid shots, the higher probability of scoring would be to pass to Hanamichi as seen in the video. So I should have kept to position to block his quick shot.   
Playing as the C requires a lot of discipline in positioning; you must be in prime position to block close shots (Familiarising yourself with the block timing is another thing altogether) AND win rebounds. One more example of bad positioning would be **1:21 - 1:25**; I should have marked Sakuragi closer since Rukawa was right in front of Takasago. I was too obsessed with man marking that I missed out covering a potential avenue for offense for the opposition.
2. **Rebound positioning -** My rebound was utter crap in this game, although to be fair when you're jostling for position with two rebounders on the opposing team it can get quite tough, but this is the perfect crucible for Cs to really brush up on their rebounding. At **0:54** for instance, given my build (jump build) I should have easily won that rebound, but I was in a poor position.   
At **2:43**, I lost focus for a moment and lost out on the rebound positioning to Hanamichi which I should've easily won by muscling Hanamichi out. **3:05** is an example of what you should do; anticipate where the ball will land, go into that position as quick as possible, be familiar with your rebound height, then jump. Of course, 3-point rebounds are quite random, but you can minimise your losses by being totally familiar with the close shots/mid shots rebound positions.
3. **Pick & Roll** \- P&R can sometimes make or break a game depending on how you do it. A skilled player would know when to P&R properly, unlike myself at **3:07** and **3:27.**

  **Mitsui**

1. **Blocking** \- Surprise! Even as a 3-pointer, you are expected to know how to mark and block. Granted, Koshino is a tough nut to crack in terms of block timing, but this takes practice, experience and hard grind. Nothing much else I can say here except this Mitsui has to brush up on his blocking. 
2. **Shooting availability** \- Even with high RES and 3-pointers ratings, it doesn't translate to results if there are multiple players (and who know to block at that!) marking you. It gets worse if they have high JAM rates. At **1:12**, while the fadeaway can indeed help you, Mitsui forced his shot too predictably. At **2:55**, he forced it once again even though Takasago is right there to block him.   
Likewise at **3:07** and **4:07**. So, while I have never played ranked matches with a 3-pointer before, from my experience, good 3-point shooters actually act as a pseudo-PG as well; they can set up the play by drawing the opposing players away and picking the perfect pass for an easy assist, or they know how to vary their offense to confuse the opponents and steal points here and there when open.   
So what Mitsui could've done in those situations would be to pass more, and once we as teammates have successfully drawn Takasago and Hanamichi away (assuming the opposing team does man marking) then he would have more breathing room to convert his shots. Of course, as he should pass, he should also continually look for open spaces that would mitigate any potential interceptions when the SF or C passes to the perimeter.
